> **Q3. TimeXer and iTransformer contain modules designed for multivariate inputs. Since lossless compression uses a univariate symbol stream, how are these models adapted and how do they function under this setting?**

Thank you for this important question. You are correct that both TimeXer and iTransformer include modules built for multivariate inputs. These modules may degrade when the task becomes single stream compression. However, **CI-based architectures naturally support the univariate case**. When the channel number equals one ($d=1$), the CI modules simply reduce to standard self-attention. **No additional adaptation is required.**

To address your concern and to evaluate these models under a setting that preserves CI structure, we conducted the **multi-stream channel independent (MSCI)** experiments. Instead of flattening, we decompose it into d independent T by 1 sequences. A single model instance processes each channel sequentially. We compress each channel independently and sum the final file sizes. During decompression we restore each channel and reconstruct the full T by d matrix without loss.

**MSCI Experimental results.**  
The MSCI setting consistently improves performance across all multivariate datasets. The compression ratios are shown below:

| Dataset   | iTransformer | TimeXer | PatchTST | SCINet | Informer | Autoformer | DLinear | LightTS |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| weather      |    **0.1581**    |  0.1651 |  0.1690  | 0.2664 |  0.2727  |   0.3078   | 0.4545  | 0.3485  |
| ETTh2        |    0.2127    |  **0.2106** |  0.2160  | 0.2203 |  0.2106  |   0.2185   | 0.2845  | 0.3121  |
| electricity  |    0.0816    |  **0.0787** |  0.0808  | 0.0873 |  0.0862  |   0.0916   | 0.1939  | 0.1487  |
| traffic      |    0.1807    |  0.1076 |  **0.1068**  | 0.1251 |  0.1293  |   0.1295   | 0.2491  | 0.2501  |

Across all datasets, **MSCI yields lower compression ratios than the single stream setting**. This indicates a clearer and more learnable structure when channels are preserved. CI based models, especially iTransformer and TimeXer, benefit the most, confirming that **their channel independent design indeed captures meaningful per channel temporal patterns**. These findings support the reviewer’s insight and validate that MSCI is a better aligned evaluation setting for multivariate architectures. We will include the full discussion in the revised version.


> **Q4. How is the relationship between lossless compression and classical time series tasks? Some baselines do not support all tasks.**

Thank you for the careful observation. The Time Series Library has formed a universal paradigm of "same backbone + task interface adaptation". Models such as iTransformer and PatchTST already connect to all the tasks for forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection and classification. Among all the models in our experiments, TimeXer and SCINet are the only two that do not support all tasks. To keep the network backbone and training settings as unchanged as possible, we followed the approach of Time Series Library and only made lightweight interface adaptation for the input, mask, and shape of different exp tasks.

The adaptation for compression uses the same idea. **The backbone remains unchanged**. We add a **linear projection that outputs 256 logits**. These logits are used by the arithmetic coder. This makes compression easy to support for most time series models, usually fewer than 20 lines of code. We have created an anonymous GitHub repository that already includes more than 10 common models with this unified interface. Anonymous GitHub: [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TSCom-Bench-8262/](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TSCom-Bench-8262/)

**I am very happy to have solved most of your concerns, and we thank you for increasing the score from 2 to 4**. For the remaining two questions (W1 and W2), our detailed answers are provided below.

> **W1. Temporal dependencies after byte-level serialization**

Thank you for pointing out this important conceptual question. We would like to clarify that **splitting each float into four IEEE-754 bytes does not destroy temporal information**, because what changes is only the representation of each value rather than the temporal order. After serialization, the byte stream remains:
$$\[
[s_{t,1},\, s_{t,2},\, s_{t,3},\, s_{t,4},\; s_{t+1,1},\, s_{t+1,2},\, \ldots],
\]$$
where $\(s_{t,i}\)$ is the $\(i\)$-th byte of $\(x_t\)$.
Since the causal timeline is preserved exactly, **seasonal cycles, long-term trends, and regime shifts continue to induce long-range dependencies** in this byte sequence. Therefore, the autoregressive model observes the same temporal context as in the original time series.

It is completely correct that two nearby floats do not share identical 4-byte patterns. For example, the real IEEE-754 encodings of:

$$\[
1.81998 \rightarrow \texttt{3F E8 F5 1B},
\]$$
$$\[
1.84561 \rightarrow \texttt{3F EC 3C F3},
\]$$

The byte results show partly differences. However, **compression does not depend on complete byte equality**. The key is that in the smooth real-world time series, **the conditional distribution of these bytes becomes highly concentrated**. In the above example, the two values share the same symbol index byte 0x3f, the second byte only changes slightly 0xe8 to 0xec, and the mantissa byte also moves in a relatively narrow and continuous area, rather than in the entire range of 0-255. This means that, according to the past time steps (e.g., the byte sequences corresponding to timesteps (t-24) and (t-1)), the model does not predict from a uniform 256 channel distribution, but from a small structured subset determined jointly by the time smoothness and the deterministic layout of IEEE-754. **The reduction of conditional entropy is the reason for better compression.**

This phenomenon is consistent with some previous work, which shows that **byte-level models can successfully learn structural patterns when ordering is preserved**. The transformer language model trained on the original UTF-8 bytes learns syntax and long-distance dependencies [1]. The audio model directly learns the frequency time structure from the PCM byte stream [2, 3]. Classical compressors and neural compressors only operate on bytes while capturing complex correlations. These results jointly confirm that **the essential structure is carried by sequence order rather than numeric format**. Our byte-level time series settings follow the same principle.

We hope that this specific example and clarification can solve this problem.

[2]Van Den Oord, A., Dieleman, S., Zen, H., Simonyan, K., Vinyals, O., Graves, A., ... & Kavukcuoglu, K. (2016). Wavenet: A generative model for raw audio. arXiv preprint arXiv:1609.03499, 12, 1.

The additional degradation from B to C shows that the models also learn the internal numeric structure formed by the exponent and mantissa bytes. These observations confirm that **byte-level encoding preserves both the temporal dependencies and the numeric structure** needed for compression based evaluation.

> **W3.2  Ablation on 16 bit, 32 bit, and 64 bit precision**

We also conducted the requested ablation. We evaluated TimeXer, PatchTST, and iTransformer under IEEE 754 formats of 16 bit, 32 bit, and 64 bit. The results are:

| Precision | TimeXer | PatchTST | iTransformer |
|:-----------:|:---------:|:-----------:|:---------------:|
| IEEE 754-16 | 0.4266 | 0.4508 | 0.4777 |
| IEEE 754-32 | 0.4040 | 0.3911 | 0.4271 |
| IEEE 754-64 | 0.5241 | 0.5264 | 0.5281 |

These results show that the framework supports all precision levels. They also show that 64 bit floats are harder to compress because the extra mantissa bytes mostly describe noise and aleatoric uncertainty. This increases entropy and reduces compressibility. In contrast 16/32 bit often compresses better because the main temporal trends are stored in the high order bytes. This confirms that our benchmark remains valid for high precision time series data and that the use of 32 bit encoding in the main experiments does not limit generality.


> **W4. Evidence for the claim that the CR of PEMS08 is close to 1 due to the .npz format**

Thank you for the suggestion. We provide stronger evidence to support this explanation. The **npz format is a compressed ZIP container** created by NumPy. As a result, the stored byte stream has **high entropy** and **almost no remaining redundancy**, which prevents further compression by any model or algorithm.

We offer two pieces of empirical evidence.

1. **General purpose compressors** such as Gzip and Zstd also report a **CR close to 1.0** on the original PEMS08 npz file. This shows that even classical engineering compressors cannot reduce its size further.

2. To verify that the issue comes from the container format rather than the dataset itself, we converted the normally compressible **Electricity** dataset into npz. Under this npz container, our benchmark also produced a **CR close to 1.0**. This confirms that the limitation is caused by the pre compressed archive rather than by our evaluation pipeline.

**As shown in our response to Q1**, once we unpack the npz file and process the raw float values, our model achieves a **substantial reduction in compressed size**. This demonstrates that the underlying data do contain temporal redundancy and that the npz container was the only factor masking compressibility.
